newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-THE FACES CHANGE BUT JUVENTUS STAY THE SAME.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-THE FACES CHANGE BUT JUVENTUS STAY THE SAME.

text.p: Juventus coach Marcello Lippi has been asked one question time and again this season. And on each occasion he has ducked it.

After the Italians ripped apart Ajax Amsterdam 4-1 and 6-2 on aggregate on Wednesday to reach a second consecutive European Cup final after last year's penalty win against the Dutch side, Lippi again faced the inevitable.
"Which is the greater team? The one that captured the title last year or this year's Juventus?," he was asked.
"It's a question I've heard so many times this season and one that I don't want to answer," he replied. "They are the same."

Courtesy to former champions such as Fabrizio Ravanelli and Gianluca Vialli aside, the team that laboured against Ajax last May and the one that demolished the Dutch team's proud away record on Wednesday are clearly different.
They still win, they still have an extraordinary team spirit but the faces are fresh.
They are also looking more impressive, despite being outplayed by Ajax for much of Wednesday's match.
Last season Juve lost 2-1 at home to Borussia Dortmund, their ultimate opponents this year, before accelerating on to the Rome final and ultimate victory.
They have not lost in Europe since and Mario Melchiot's 75th minute goal for Ajax on Wednesday was the first they have conceded in this year's tournament at home.
"I'll repeat what I said after the home leg," said Ajax coach Louis Van Gaal. "I have never met opponents who have beaten us like Juventus did."
Former Ajax great Johan Cruyff, present as a television commentator, was equally impressed.

"Lippi's team is a truly Italian one," he said. "I like this team because, among those at the top in Europe, they do not appear to have been affected by the craze for foreigners. They are my favourites to win in Munich."
In the space of 12 months, by selling three of their biggest names abroad and buying carefully mostly on the Italian market, Juventus have undergone a quiet revolution.

Last season they won the cup while losing the domestic league title. This year, their 100th anniversary as a club, they could be Italian, European and world club champions -- a feat only Inter, who did it in 1965, have achieved.

At the Delle Alpi stadium on Wednesday night, there were only three players -- goalkeeper Angelo Peruzzi, defender Ciro Ferrara and French midfielder Didier Deschamps -- in the starting line-up who also played in Rome.
In Germany on May 28, against Borussia Dortmund, they could face four of their former players, including Portugal's Paulo Sousa whom they sold after last year's win.
"I have no doubt that Juventus will win," said Ajax's Frank De Boer. "I can't remember when Ajax last let in four goals in a European Cup match. They are from another planet."
The goalscorers in Turin were Christian Vieri, French midfielder Zinedine Zidane, Attilio Lombardo and Nicola Amoruso while Croat Alen Boksic had a goal disallowed.
Only Lombardo was at the club last season and, at 31 years of age, his role then as now was more of a super-sub.
Vieri, at Atalanta last season, has emerged as a full Italian international at the age of 23 and has now scored four goals in the European Cup campaign.
Zidane, after a difficult start in Italy, is growing in stature by the day as the most popular French player at the club since the days of the great Michel Platini.

The shy Frenchman laid on two of the goals on Wednesday and scored another solo one that had Ajax coach Louis Van Gaal covering him with praise and the fans bellowing his name in what amounted to a popular coronation for King "Zizou".
"These players here are exceptional. We have a group of people who are truly great," said Lippi.
